patient.chief_complaint: Two weeks of bizarre behavior, inability to sleep, new facial tics and seizures
patient.history_present_illness: A 23-year-old right-handed woman was brought to the emergency department by her parents who report a 2-week history of frightening behavioral and neurological deterioration. Approximately 4 weeks prior to the current presentation, the patient had a febrile illness lasting 6 days with documented temperatures up to 39.1, headache, neck stiffness (which resolved), and fatigue. She was evaluated at an urgent care center where no lumbar puncture was performed; she was given oral ibuprofen and told to rest. She appeared to recover fully and was back at work after one week. The current illness began insidiously approximately 2 weeks ago: first with difficulty sleeping, then with progressive personality change that her parents describe as 'not recognizing her own daughter' — she became fearful, had unprovoked outbursts of laughter, and started making bizarre statements such as claiming the family's cats were 'sending her messages.' Over the following week her parents noticed she would suddenly stop mid-sentence and stare blankly, then resume speaking without remembering the interruption. Simultaneously she developed involuntary repetitive facial movements — constant chewing motions, tongue protrusion, and grimacing. She had one fall with jerking of all four limbs five days ago, and on the day of presentation had a 2-minute witnessed GTCS. Her parents note she has barely slept in the last 10 days. On arrival she is markedly tachycardic and hypertensive, diaphoretic, and intermittently combative. She weighs 6 kg less than her baseline weight (per her mother) due to refusal to eat.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Severely encephalopathic. Intermittently agitated and then somnolent. Not oriented to person, place, or time. Continuous orofacial dyskinesias — repetitive chewing, lip-smacking, grimacing. Occasional echolalia. Intermittent unintelligible moaning.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4mm bilaterally, reactive. Continuous perioral and tongue movements. Mild hypersalivation.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral distal choreoathetosis. Bilateral upper extremity posturing briefly during examination. Tone mildly increased.
neurological_exam.additional: Autonomic instability: HR 138, BP 172/108, temp 38.4, diaphoresis. No meningismus on passive exam.

Bilateral basal ganglia signal change is one imaging feature seen in CJD; however CJD typically shows asymmetric, rapidly progressive cortical ribboning and DWI restriction — features not present here. Clinical correlation required.

results.title: Bilateral teratoma in anti-NMDAR encephalitis: case series
results.key_finding: Bilateral teratomas occur in ~10% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases; bilateral resection associated with better outcomes than unilateral resection alone

output.summary: Bilateral ovarian teratomas occur in approximately 10% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases with teratoma. Both teratomas should be resected. Bilateral resection is associated with improved neurological outcomes compared to unilateral resection alone. If fertility preservation is desired, cystectomy rather than oophorectomy is preferred when technically feasible.

key_reasoning_points: Bilateral ovarian teratomas in ~10% of anti-NMDAR encephalitis cases with teratoma — both must be identified and resected
Very high antibody titer (serum 1:1024) indicates extremely severe disease — early ICU admission appropriate
Basal ganglia involvement on MRI correlates with the dyskinesias and choreoathetosis
Severe SIADH (Na 124) contributes to seizure risk and must be managed carefully
Febrile illness with neck stiffness 4 weeks prior may have been an early meningitic presentation triggering the autoimmune response
